conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the decisive fork governing every nutritional decision?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Choose the least invasive route the gut can tolerate ("if the gut works, use it").

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is oral support used, and does it require a working gut?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Used when the patient can swallow safely. Requires a working gut: Yes.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is enteral (tube) feeding used, and does it require a working gut?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Used when there is unsafe/inadequate oral intake but a functional GI tract. Requires a working gut: Yes.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is parenteral (IV) nutrition used, and does it require a working gut?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Used when the GI tract is non-functional, inaccessible, or perforated. Requires a working gut: No.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Who is screened for malnutrition and how often (NICE CG32)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Screen all inpatients on admission and outpatients at first appointment. Repeat weekly for inpatients. Tool = MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What criteria define a patient as malnourished (any one of)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: BMI <18.5; unintentional weight loss >10% in 3–6 months; or BMI <20 + weight loss >5% in 3–6 months.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What criteria define a patient as at risk of malnutrition (any of)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Eaten little/nothing for >5 days (or likely to for the next 5+); poor absorption or high losses; increased needs from catabolism.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the daily nutritional targets (not severely ill, no refeeding risk)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Energy: 25–35 kcal/kg (lower if BMI >25). Protein: 0.8–1.5 g/kg. Fluid: 30–35 mL/kg (+ extra for drains/fistulae). Plus electrolytes, minerals, micronutrients, fibre.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are targets adjusted for a seriously ill patient or one nil by mouth >5 days?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Start at ≤50% of target for the first 1–2 days, then build up.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What two conditions must both hold for enteral tube feeding to be indicated?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: (1) Inadequate or unsafe oral intake AND (2) a functional, accessible GI tract.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is an NG tube — site, when used, and key points?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Site: stomach (nasal). Use when: short-term (<4 weeks). Key points: most common; allows bolus + hypertonic feeds; easily displaced.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is an NJ tube — site, when used, and key points?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Site: jejunum (nasal). Use when: short-term + delayed gastric emptying / reflux risk. Key points: reduces aspiration risk; post-pyloric placement can be difficult.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a PEG — site, when used, and key points?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Site: stomach (percutaneous). Use when: long-term (≥4 weeks). Key points: stroke, MND, Parkinson's, oesophageal cancer; placed endoscopically under antibiotic cover; usable 4 h after insertion.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a PEJ / jejunostomy — site, when used, and key points?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Site: jejunum (percutaneous). Use when: long-term + high reflux/aspiration risk. Key points: permits early post-op feeding; more technically demanding.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 4-week rule for feeding routes?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: <4 weeks → NG. ≥4 weeks → consider PEG. The single most-tested route rule.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the NG safety rule (NPSA) for confirming tube position?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Confirm position after placement and before every use — aspirate pH ≤5.5 on pH paper. X-ray if pH equivocal. A misplaced NG into the lung is a Never Event.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does the duration of parenteral nutrition determine the access line?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: <14 days, no other central need → peripheral venous catheter (mind pH/tonicity). <30 days → non-tunnelled central catheter. >30 days (long-term) → tunnelled subclavian line. TPN is typically via a central line — the hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the complications of parenteral nutrition?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Line sepsis — the big one (daily catheter-site inspection); thrombosis; refeeding syndrome; deranged LFTs / cholestasis; electrolyte and glucose disturbance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is trophic feeding and why is it used alongside PN?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Keep minimal enteral feeding alongside PN where possible → maintains gut function, reduces cholestasis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism of refeeding syndrome?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Carbohydrate load → insulin surge → rapid intracellular electrolyte shift → ↓phosphate (cardinal), ↓K+, ↓Mg2+ + expanding ECF volume. Thiamine demand spikes.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the cardinal electrolyte abnormality of refeeding syndrome, and the consequences?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: ↓Phosphate is cardinal (with ↓K+, ↓Mg2+). Consequences: cardiac/respiratory failure, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, coma.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the high-risk criteria for refeeding syndrome where ONE alone is sufficient (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: BMI <16; weight loss >15% in 3–6 months; little/no intake >10 days; low K+/PO4(3-)/Mg2+ before feeding.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the high-risk criteria for refeeding syndrome where TWO are needed (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: BMI <18.5; weight loss >10%; little/no intake >5 days; alcohol or drug history (including insulin, chemo, antacids, diuretics).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is feeding started and built up to prevent refeeding syndrome (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Start at max 10 kcal/kg/day (5 kcal/kg in extreme cases, BMI <14). Build to full needs over 4–7 days.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What thiamine/vitamin and electrolyte management is needed in refeeding syndrome (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Thiamine 200–300 mg/day + vitamin B co strong — before and during the first 10 days. Replace K+, PO4(3-), Mg2+ as needed; do NOT pre-correct electrolytes before starting feeding.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the tube-related complications of enteral feeding (NG vs PEG)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: NG: discomfort, sinusitis, erosions; bronchial misplacement (fatal if used). PEG: stoma infection, peritonitis, dislodgement.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are blockage and infection prevented in enteral feeding?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Blockage: flush with water before and after every use. Infection: discard feed sets every 24 h.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is aspiration minimised during enteral feeding?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Nurse at ≥30° during and after feeding; use post-pyloric tubes for flat patients.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are GI symptoms (bloating, diarrhoea, nausea) managed in enteral feeding?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Slow the rate or switch to continuous feed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What bloods are monitored during feeding, and how often initially?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Bloods (daily until stable): U&Es, glucose, Mg, phosphate, LFTs/INR, calcium, albumin, CRP. Trace elements (Zn, Cu, Se) periodically on long-term PN.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What clinical and route-specific monitoring is done during feeding?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Clinical: weight, BMI, fluid balance, GI tolerance, tube/stoma site. NG: pH check before every feed. PN lines: daily site inspection for infection.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Is clinically assisted nutrition and hydration (CANH) a treatment or basic care, and what governs the decision?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: CANH is a medical treatment — not basic care. It can be withheld or withdrawn like any treatment, using the same consent framework. Capacity drives the decision.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is a CANH decision made depending on capacity?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A competent patient's refusal must be respected. If they lack capacity, decide in best interests (advance directives, MDT, family).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the goal of pre-operative management, and what are its key domains?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: It optimises the patient's condition before surgery to minimise perioperative risk, translating pre-operative assessment findings into action. Key domains: consent, fasting, medication management, DVT prophylaxis, bowel prep, skin prep, and same-day checks.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does valid consent require under the MCA 2005?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Capacity (understand, retain, weigh, communicate the decision); voluntary (free from coercion); informed (material risks, benefits, alternatives explained); written consent (form 1/3) for procedures under GA or significant risk; obtained by the surgeon or a trainee supervised by the surgeon.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the four components of capacity?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Understand, retain, weigh, and communicate the decision.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What did the Montgomery ruling (2015) establish about consent?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: The patient must be told of ALL material risks — those a reasonable patient would want to know, or that this specific patient would consider significant. It replaces the old Bolam standard for consent; the surgeon must tailor the risk discussion to the individual and document the discussion, not just the signature.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is consent handled when capacity is lacking, for elective vs emergency surgery?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Act in best interests (MCA). Elective surgery: delay until capacity returns if possible. Emergency: proceed in best interests — consult next of kin (advisory, not legally binding) + document + consider an IMCA.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is pre-operative fasting necessary, and what does modern practice avoid?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Fasting prevents pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents (Mendelson's syndrome). Modern guidelines avoid prolonged starvation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 2-4-6 fasting rule?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Clear fluids (water, clear juice, tea/coffee without milk): 2 hours. Breast milk: 4 hours. Formula / cow's milk / solids: 6 hours.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is carbohydrate loading, its benefits, and contraindications?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: 400 mL complex carbohydrate drink the night before + 200 mL up to 2 h pre-op (ERAS protocol). Reduces insulin resistance, anxiety, and post-op nausea. Contraindicated in diabetics and those with gastroparesis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are antihypertensives (ACEi, ARB) and diuretics managed perioperatively, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Antihypertensives (ACEi, ARB): withhold the morning of surgery (risk of refractory intra-op hypotension with anaesthesia). Diuretics: withhold the morning of surgery (risk of hypovolaemia + electrolyte disturbance).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are beta-blockers managed perioperatively, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Continue — sudden withdrawal → rebound tachycardia / MI.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is metformin managed perioperatively, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Withhold on the day of surgery (and 48 h after if contrast is used) — risk of lactic acidosis if renal impairment / contrast.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is insulin managed perioperatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Adjust per the local VRIII (sliding scale) protocol — NBM status alters the requirement.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is warfarin managed perioperatively, and what is the target INR?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Stop 5 days pre-op; bridge with LMWH if high thrombotic risk. Target INR <1.5 for surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are DOACs managed perioperatively, and why the caution?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Stop 24–48 h pre-op (48 h if CrCl <50 for dabigatran). No reversal agent available routinely (except idarucizumab for dabigatran).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are antiplatelet agents (aspirin/clopidogrel) managed perioperatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Continue aspirin if low bleeding risk; stop clopidogrel 5–7 days pre-op if possible. Balance: thrombotic risk (coronary stents) vs bleeding risk.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are the OCP/HRT managed perioperatively, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Stop 4 weeks before major surgery (↑ DVT risk); restart once mobile.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are long-term steroids managed perioperatively, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Continue + give perioperative steroid cover — HPA axis suppression → adrenal crisis risk if omitted.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are SSRIs/MAOIs managed perioperatively, and what is the risk?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Usually continue; avoid serotonergic drugs intra-op. Serotonin syndrome risk with pethidine, tramadol.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Who needs VTE risk assessment, and why does it matter?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: All surgical patients must have a VTE risk assessment (NICE NG89). DVT + PE = the leading cause of preventable hospital death.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanical VTE prophylaxis for surgical patients?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: TED stockings (thigh-length) — all patients; intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) — intra-op + post-op until mobile (especially orthopaedic, major abdominal surgery); early mobilisation; adequate hydration.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (LMWH) started, and for how long?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Start 6–12 h post-op (once haemostasis confirmed). Duration 7–10 days standard; 28 days for major abdominal/pelvic cancer surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is pharmacological VTE prophylaxis withheld or dose-adjusted?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Withhold if: epidural in-situ (wait 12 h after removal), active bleeding, platelets <50. Renal dose adjustment if eGFR <30 (use unfractionated heparin).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the high-risk factors on VTE risk tools (e.g. Caprini)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Malignancy, previous VTE, thrombophilia, immobility, BMI >30, major pelvic/lower limb surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the general principles of perioperative diabetes management?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Schedule first on the morning list where possible (minimises fasting time); target BM 6–10 mmol/L perioperatively (avoid hypo- and hyperglycaemia); check BM 2-hourly whilst NBM; involve the diabetic specialist nurse / endocrine team.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is a VRIII (variable rate insulin infusion) indicated, and what fluid is it run alongside?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Indicated in T1DM; T2DM on insulin; major surgery; BM uncontrolled pre-op. Run alongside 5% glucose + 0.45% NaCl + 0.15% KCl. Avoid plain 0.9% saline — causes hyperchloraemic acidosis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is a patient monitored on a VRIII, and when is it stopped?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Monitor BM hourly on the VRIII; electrolytes 4–6 hourly. Convert back to S/C insulin at the first meal.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Is routine mechanical bowel prep recommended, and when is it still used?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Routine mechanical bowel prep is NOT recommended for most colorectal surgery (ERAS/NICE evidence: no mortality/anastomotic leak benefit, causes dehydration). Still used for: left colonic anastomoses (some centres), rectal surgery, laparoscopic colectomy with intra-op colonoscopy. Oral antibiotics (erythromycin + neomycin) ± IV antibiotics at induction for colorectal cases.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What skin prep agent is preferred for SSI prevention, and how is hair removed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Chlorhexidine 2% in 70% alcohol — superior to povidone-iodine for SSI prevention (NICE NG125). Hair removal: clippers NOT razor (razors cause micro-abrasions → ↑ SSI).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When are prophylactic antibiotics given for SSI prevention, and what else reduces SSI?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Prophylactic antibiotics at induction (not before, not >30 min after). Maintain normothermia (warm air blanket, warm IV fluids) and normoglycaemia (↑ glucose → ↑ SSI risk).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is ERAS, and for which surgery is it now standard?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery — a multimodal protocol across pre-, intra-, and post-operative phases. Reduces complications, length of stay, and costs. Now standard for colorectal, orthopaedic, and major abdominal surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the pre-operative ERAS elements?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Patient education and goal-setting; prehabilitation (exercise, nutrition, smoking cessation); carbohydrate loading; avoid prolonged fasting/bowel prep; anaemia correction (IV iron if Hb <130 g/L and surgery >4 weeks away); VTE prophylaxis planning.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the intra/post-operative ERAS elements?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Short-acting anaesthetic agents (LMA preferred); laparoscopic approach where possible; goal-directed fluid therapy (avoid over/under-hydration); epidural/regional anaesthesia to reduce opioids; early feeding (day of surgery or day 1); early mobilisation; avoid NGT, urinary catheter, drains if not required.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is checked at "Sign in" (before induction) on the WHO checklist?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Patient identity + consent confirmed, site marked, allergies, anaesthetic equipment checked, pulse oximetry working.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is checked at "Time out" (before skin incision) on the WHO checklist?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: All team members introduced, patient/site/procedure confirmed, antibiotic given, imaging displayed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is checked at "Sign out" (before leaving theatre) on the WHO checklist?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Swab/instrument/sharps count correct, specimens labelled, equipment problems noted, recovery plan discussed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What impact did the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (2009) have?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: It reduced major complications by 36% and mortality by 47% in the original study. Now mandatory in all NHS theatres.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the decisive fork that governs the entire acute GI bleed workup, and what divides it?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Upper vs lower, divided by the ligament of Treitz.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Define an upper GI bleed by site, and how is it triaged?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Oesophagus, stomach or duodenum (proximal to the ligament of Treitz). Triaged to endoscopy (OGD).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Define a lower GI bleed by site, and how is it triaged?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Below the ligament of Treitz. Triaged to imaging / colonoscopy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the safety rule for a haemodynamically unstable patient with a large fresh PR bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: They have an upper GI bleed until proven otherwise (a brisk upper bleed transits fast and presents as fresh rectal blood).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What vocabulary points to an upper vs a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Haematemesis / "coffee-ground" vomit + melaena → upper. Haematochezia (fresh PR blood) → usually lower.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the "resuscitate first" universal principle in an acute GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Unstable bleeds need urgent resuscitation, wide-bore IV access and blood products until stable; activate the major haemorrhage protocol; correct coagulopathy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the "FBC trap" in an acute GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Acute bleeds may NOT initially show anaemia — Hb concentration lags (takes time to haemodilute), so a normal Hb never reassures in an acute bleed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does the urea:creatinine ratio help localise a GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A raised urea:creatinine ratio points to an upper source (digested blood is a protein load absorbed in the gut, so a raised urea with normal creatinine points to an upper GI source).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the causes of an upper GI bleed and their approximate frequencies?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Peptic ulcer disease 62% (commonest); AVMs/angiodysplasia 10%; gastritis/duodenitis 8%; oesophageal varices 6%; Mallory-Weiss tear, malignancy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the decisive sub-fork in an upper GI bleed, and why does it matter?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Variceal vs non-variceal — it changes the drugs entirely.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the clinical features of an upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Haematemesis, "coffee-ground" vomit, melaena (black tarry stool — digested blood), epigastric pain (ulcer), signs of chronic liver disease (varices).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What bloods are sent in an upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: FBC, U&Es, LFTs, coagulation screen, group & save / crossmatch; VBG + lactate.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the urea clue in an upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Urea is disproportionately raised relative to creatinine — digested blood is a protein load absorbed in the gut, so a raised urea with normal creatinine points to an upper GI source.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Glasgow-Blatchford score (GBS) — when is it used and its purpose?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Used pre-endoscopy. A score of 0 = very low risk → consider outpatient / early discharge (uses Hb, urea, SBP, HR, melaena, syncope, liver disease, heart failure).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Rockall score — when is it used and its purpose?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Used post-endoscopy. Predicts rebleeding and mortality (age, shock, comorbidity, diagnosis, endoscopic stigmata).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the OGD timing in an upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Within 24 hours; within 2 hours if variceal or haemodynamically unstable, after resuscitation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is a non-variceal upper GI bleed managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Endoscopic haemostasis — clips or thermal coagulation. PPI AFTER endoscopy, not before (NICE 2016) — then IV PPI (omeprazole 80 mg bolus, then 8 mg/h for 72 h post-haemostasis).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is a PPI given in a non-variceal upper GI bleed, and what is the regimen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: PPI AFTER endoscopy, not before (NICE 2016) — IV PPI (omeprazole 80 mg bolus, then 8 mg/h for 72 h post-haemostasis).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the three-part bundle for a variceal upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Terlipressin IV + prophylactic antibiotics + urgent endoscopic band ligation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the management if endoscopy fails to control an upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: CT mesenteric angiography to identify/control the source → guide embolisation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the causes of a lower GI bleed and their approximate frequencies?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Diverticular disease 40% (commonest); colitis/IBD 21%; neoplasia 14%; coagulopathic 12%; angiodysplasia, haemorrhoids, ischaemic colitis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Are diverticular bleeds painful, and how does this differ from diverticulitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Diverticulosis is the commonest cause; diverticular bleeds are often painless, but bleeds from diverticulitis can be painful.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is angiodysplasia, where do AVMs form, and what bleeds does it cause?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: The most common vascular abnormality of the GI tract; AVMs form most often in the caecum and ascending colon. It is the 2nd commonest cause of rectal bleeding in over-60s and the commonest cause of small-bowel bleeding.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does angiodysplasia present and behave?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Presents as painless occult / recurrent PR bleeding; stops spontaneously in >90% but often recurs.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the associations of angiodysplasia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Aortic stenosis (Heyde's syndrome), chronic renal failure, von Willebrand disease.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is angiodysplasia managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Argon plasma coagulation (APC); capsule endoscopy preferred for small-bowel lesions.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is Heyde's syndrome?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Aortic stenosis + angiodysplasia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does the character of haematochezia suggest about the cause of a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Haematochezia (fresh/maroon PR blood); painless suggests diverticular/angiodysplasia, painful suggests colitis/ischaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What examination do all patients with a lower GI bleed need, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A DRE + proctoscopy — to exclude a bedside-treatable anorectal source (haemorrhoids).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the risk factors for an adverse outcome in a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Haemodynamic instability, ongoing haematochezia, age >60, creatinine >150, significant comorbidities.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does the Oakland score do in a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Stratifies whether outpatient management is feasible (age, sex, previous LGIB admissions, PR findings, HR, SBP, Hb).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What bloods are sent as a minimum in a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: FBC, U&Es, LFT, clotting and Group & Save as a minimum; stool cultures to exclude infective causes.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the stability-driven imaging fork for a stable (~80%) lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Mild & self-limiting → colonoscopy once stable + bowel-prepped (diagnostic + therapeutic).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the stability-driven imaging fork for an unstable lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Resuscitate + correct coagulopathy + major haemorrhage protocol, then urgent CT angiogram BEFORE any endoscopic therapy → permits IR embolisation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What if colonoscopy is negative in a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Do an OGD to look for an upper source; if still inconclusive → capsule endoscopy or RBC scintigraphy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What proportion of lower GI bleeds settle spontaneously, and what does this allow?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: ~80% (up to ~85%) settle spontaneously — stable, low-risk young patients in whom bleeding has stopped can be discharged for outpatient investigation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the management options for a lower GI bleed (endoscopic, IR, surgery)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Endoscopic therapy (clips, thermal, APC for angiodysplasia, band ligation); IR embolisation (via CT angiogram) for ongoing bleeding not controlled endoscopically; surgery = last resort (unstable despite resuscitation, or failed endoscopic/IR control).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is an unstable lower GI bleed managed in terms of pathway, and what proportion settle?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Unstable lower bleed → CT angiogram before endoscopy → IR embolisation. Overall ~80% of lower GI bleeds settle spontaneously, but an unstable bleed needs active intervention.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Erosive gastritis/duodenitis causes ~8% of upper GI bleeds. Name the two eponymous stress ulcers and their triggers.
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Curling's ulcer = severe burns (gastric mucosal ischaemia); Cushing's ulcer = head injury / raised ICP (vagal overstimulation → excess acid).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Who should receive stress ulcer prophylaxis to prevent GI bleeding, and with what?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: The critically ill — major burns, head injury, mechanical ventilation for over 48 hours, coagulopathy. Give a PPI or an H2-receptor antagonist.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the initial priority and decisive fork in the acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Sudden onset of severe abdominal pain. Initial priority: A–E, obs, resuscitate first, then take a history. The decisive fork: urgent intervention now (bleed/perforation/ischaemia) vs further investigation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the three "must not miss" emergencies in the acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Acute bleeding, perforated viscus, and ischaemic bowel.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: For acute bleeding: worst cause, cardinal clue, key bloods, and definitive investigation?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Worst cause: ruptured AAA → vascular team. Cardinal clue: hypovolaemic shock (tachy, hypotension, pale). Key bloods: ↓ Hb. Definitive Ix: CT angiography.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: For perforated viscus: worst causes, cardinal clue, key bloods, and definitive investigation?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Worst causes: peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, IBD. Cardinal clue: peritonism ± rigid abdomen. Key bloods: ↑ WCC/CRP. Definitive Ix: erect CXR (free air) / CT.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: For ischaemic bowel: worst cause, cardinal clue, key bloods, and definitive investigation?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Worst cause: acute mesenteric ischaemia. Cardinal clue: pain out of proportion to exam. Key bloods: ↑ lactate, metabolic acidosis. Definitive Ix: CT angiography.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for right hypochondriac pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Gallstones, cholangitis, hepatitis — plus cardiac/lung referred pain (always consider the chest).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for epigastric pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Oesophagitis, peptic/perforated ulcer, pancreatitis, MI (referred).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for left hypochondriac pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Splenic abscess, splenomegaly, rupture.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for right/left lumbar pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Ureteric colic, pyelonephritis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for umbilical pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Appendicitis (early), mesenteric lymphadenitis, Meckel's.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for right iliac fossa pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Appendicitis, Crohn's, caecal obstruction, ovarian cyst, ectopic pregnancy, hernia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for hypogastric pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Testicular torsion, urinary retention, cystitis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for left iliac fossa pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Diverticulitis, UC, constipation, ovarian cyst.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the distinguisher for biliary colic vs acute cholecystitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Biliary colic: post-fatty meal; no fever, normal markers. Acute cholecystitis: Murphy's sign +ve, fever, ↑ CRP.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the distinguisher for ascending cholangitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Charcot's triad: RUQ pain + fever + jaundice.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the distinguisher for pancreatitis (hepatobiliary table)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Epigastric → back; ↑ amylase (>3× ULN).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the lower GI differentials and their distinguishing features?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Appendicitis — central → RIF, anorexia, low-grade fever, Rovsing's sign. Diverticulitis — LIF colicky pain, fever, ↑ WCC. Obstruction — central colicky pain, no bowels/flatus, tinkling sounds.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How do peptic ulcers present, and how do duodenal vs gastric ulcers relate to eating?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Peptic ulcer — epigastric, NSAID/alcohol history. Duodenal ulcer: relieved by eating. Gastric ulcer: worsened by eating.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the medical mimics of an acute abdomen that you should NOT operate on?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: MI (epigastric referred pain; always do an ECG); DKA, Addisonian crisis; porphyria, lead poisoning; lower-lobe pneumonia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the urological differentials and their distinguishing features?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Renal colic — loin → groin, severe/intermittent, haematuria. Pyelonephritis — loin pain, fever/rigors. Urinary retention — suprapubic, male/BPH.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is mandatory in all reproductive-age women with an acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A urine pregnancy test (mandatory).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does an ectopic pregnancy present?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: RIF/LIF pain, 6–9 weeks amenorrhoea, ± PV bleed; risk of rupture.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the other gynaecological differentials in the acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Ovarian cyst torsion, PID.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the vascular differentials and their distinguishing features?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Ruptured AAA — central → back, collapse, pulsatile mass. Mesenteric ischaemia — AF/CVD history, pain out of proportion, ↑ lactate.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What investigations make up the acute abdomen work-up?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Urine dip + MC&S; pregnancy test (all reproductive-age women); ECG (exclude MI as epigastric pain cause); ABG/VBG (↑ lactate = ischaemia; metabolic alkalosis = vomiting); FBC (↓Hb / ↑WCC), U&E, LFT, CRP, amylase (>3× ULN = pancreatitis), INR, calcium; erect CXR (free air under diaphragm = perforation); CT abdo/pelvis (perforation, obstruction, ischaemia); USS (biliary tree, renal tract, uterus/adnexa).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the initial management bundle for the acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A–E; alert seniors early in the unwell patient. NBM if surgery likely or obstruction. NG tube if obstruction. IV fluids if hypovolaemia. IV antibiotics if infection/sepsis. Analgesia (IV morphine titrated), anti-emetics. VTE assessment + LMWH prophylaxis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does pain out of proportion to examination signify until proven otherwise?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Mesenteric ischaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the three classic named signs and their conditions?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Charcot's triad = cholangitis. Murphy's = cholecystitis. Rovsing's = appendicitis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the classic pain-migration patterns in the acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Appendicitis: umbilicus → RIF. Renal colic: loin → groin. AAA/pancreatitis: → back.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the ulcer food rule, and what do the key bloods indicate?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Duodenal = relieved by food; gastric = worsened by food. Key bloods: amylase >3× ULN = pancreatitis; ↑ lactate = ischaemia; ↓ Hb = bleed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is acute appendicitis, where is the appendix, what is the peak age, and which group is the can't-miss high-risk group?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Inflammation of the appendix — a blind-ended tube from the caecum where the three taeniae coli converge. Peak age is the second decade (~10–20 years, into the early 20s); children are the can't-miss high-risk group (atypical presentation + high perforation risk).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the decisive cascade in appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Luminal obstruction → trapped secretions → infection & inflammation → gangrene → rupture → peritonitis. The timeline drives urgency.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the causes of luminal obstruction in appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Faecolith (compacted faecal stone — classic); lymphoid hyperplasia (commoner in younger patients, post-viral); undigested seeds/impacted stool; caecal tumour (the can't-miss cause in older patients).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the cardinal pain pattern of appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Starts central/peri-umbilical (dull, poorly localised — visceral midgut pain) → migrates to RIF (sharp, well localised — parietal peritoneal inflammation). Worse on coughing / speed bumps.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the significance of vomiting timing relative to pain in appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Pain-first = appendicitis order; vomiting-first = gastroenteritis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key symptoms of appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Pain — central → RIF migration (key feature); vomiting after pain; anorexia, nausea; constipation > diarrhoea (pelvic appendicitis → rectal irritation / loose stool).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the examination findings in appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: McBurney's point tenderness; rebound + percussion tenderness + guarding → peritonism; RIF mass → appendiceal abscess; sepsis signs in severe cases (tachycardia, hypotension); Rovsing's sign (LIF palpation → RIF pain); psoas sign (RIF pain on right hip extension → retrocaecal appendix).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is Rovsing's sign?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: LIF palpation → RIF pain.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the psoas sign, and what does it indicate?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: RIF pain on right hip extension → a retrocaecal appendix.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why are children atypical and high-risk in appendicitis, and what should be examined?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: They often present with diarrhoea, urinary symptoms, or left-sided pain. Examine GI, urinary AND genitals in all boys (exclude testicular torsion). A child <6 years with symptoms >48 hours = high perforation risk → active observation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the adult differentials for RIF pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Gynaecological — ovarian cyst rupture, ectopic pregnancy, PID; renal — ureteric colic, UTI, pyelonephritis; GI — Crohn's, Meckel's diverticulum, diverticular disease; urological — testicular torsion, epididymo-orchitis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the paediatric differentials for appendicitis, and which is the commonest mimic?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Mesenteric adenitis — inflamed mesenteric nodes, often post-URTI/tonsillitis; the commonest paediatric mimic. Also gastroenteritis, constipation, intussusception, UTI, and testicular torsion (boys).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: If the appendix is normal at operation, what should be inspected and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Inspect the distal ileum for an inflamed Meckel's diverticulum — a congenital blind-ended diverticulum ~60 cm from the ileocaecal valve that can inflame, rupture, or cause volvulus/intussusception.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Is appendicitis a clinical or imaging diagnosis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Appendicitis is a clinical diagnosis. Raised inflammatory markers + clinical findings = sufficient to warrant appendicectomy. Imaging only if features are inconclusive.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What blood tests are used in appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: FBC + CRP + G&S: neutrophil-predominant leucocytosis; ↑ CRP. G&S if surgical intervention is planned.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the role of urine dip and pregnancy test in suspected appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Urinalysis to exclude renal/urological causes. Serum hCG (pregnancy test) is mandatory in all reproductive-age women — exclude ectopic.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is imaging (USS/CT) used in appendicitis, and which is preferred in women and children?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: USS/CT if equivocal. USS first if gynaecological differentials (especially transvaginal USS). USS preferred over CT in children (avoid radiation). CT if diagnosis remains unclear.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the gold-standard surgical management of appendicitis, and what is preferred in pregnancy?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Laparoscopic appendicectomy — gold standard; inspect the whole abdomen for other pathology. Open (Lanz incision) — preferred in pregnancy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the gold-standard surgical management of appendicitis, and what is the approach in pregnancy?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Laparoscopic appendicectomy — the gold standard; inspect the whole abdomen for other pathology. In pregnancy, laparoscopic appendicectomy is now considered safe in all trimesters (RCOG) and is increasingly preferred; an open/muscle-splitting (Lanz) approach remains an alternative, especially in advanced pregnancy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is an appendiceal mass managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: IV antibiotics + interval appendicectomy 6–8 weeks later.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is a pelvic abscess (special scenario) managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Fever + RIF mass; confirmed on CT; managed with antibiotics + percutaneous drainage.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the status of antibiotic-only management for appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A growing evidence base for selected uncomplicated adults; surgery remains gold standard but it is increasingly an examined alternative.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the most serious complication of appendicitis, and what are its signs?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Perforation: peritoneal contamination → generalised peritonitis, especially in children with delayed presentation (>48 h). Signs: sudden pain relief then worsening, rigid abdomen, sepsis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is an appendiceal mass (complication), and how does a pelvic abscess complication present?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Appendiceal mass — omentum + small bowel wall off the appendix. Pelvic abscess — fever + a palpable RIF mass; CT-confirmed; IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the other complications of appendicitis besides perforation, mass and pelvic abscess?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Surgical site infection; stump appendicitis (rare — if insufficient appendix removed).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is the caecal tumour an important cause in older patients with appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: It is the obstructing cause in older patients — always send the appendix for histopathology.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the purpose of pre-operative assessment, and what is the ideal timing?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: To identify comorbidities that risk complications during anaesthesia, surgery, or recovery. Timing: 2–4 weeks before surgery (leaves time to optimise).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does urgency dictate the depth of pre-operative optimisation?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Elective surgery → delay and optimise (e.g. poorly controlled diabetes). Emergency surgery → proceed with whatever optimisation time allows.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is screened in the cardiovascular system pre-operatively, and what is the key predictor?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: HTN; exercise tolerance = the key predictor of post-op complications; red-flag undiagnosed disease (exertional chest pain, syncope, orthopnoea).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is screened in the respiratory system pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Adequate oxygenation/ventilation (↓ peri-op ischaemia); OSA; can they lie flat / chronic cough? — these may preclude spinal anaesthesia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is screened in the renal and endocrine systems pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Renal: baseline function + renal-specific meds. Endocrine: especially diabetes and thyroid disease.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why does GORD matter pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Aspiration of gastric contents can be fatal → it alters the anaesthetic technique.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What pregnancy and sickle cell considerations apply pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Pregnancy: a urinary pregnancy test is mandatory in all reproductive-age women. Sickle cell: consider if born somewhere without routine newborn screening.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is covered in the past surgical and anaesthetic history?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Past surgical history — what/when/why; repeat procedures change operative time & difficulty (adhesions). Past anaesthetic history — prior operations, anaesthetic type, any problems.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is covered in the drug, family and social history pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Drug history — full list (some need stopping/changing) + drug & non-drug allergies. Family history — general + FHx of anaesthetic problems (especially malignant hyperthermia). Social history — smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs; language/interpreter need; living situation (discharge planning).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What family history is a key anaesthetic red flag?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A family history of anaesthetic problems, especially malignant hyperthermia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does the pre-operative examination involve?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: General examination — uncover undiagnosed pathology; airway examination — predict difficulty of airway management (intubation); ± operation-relevant area if appropriate.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is MRSA swabbing done in all patients, and how is a positive result managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: MRSA swabs in all patients — nostril + perineum; positive → decontamination wash + nasal ointment (before theatre).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When are urinalysis, ECG, and CXR done as routine pre-operative investigations?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Urinalysis — suspected UTI. ECG — CVD history or major surgery. CXR — only when necessary.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is an FBC and U&Es done pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: FBC: anaemia/thrombocytopenia → correct or prepare blood products. U&Es: baseline renal function → fluids & drugs (avoid morphine in CKD).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why are LFTs, HbA1c, and TFTs done pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: LFTs: liver metabolism & synthetic function. HbA1c: diabetes — glycaemic control. TFTs: thyroid disease.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is a clotting screen done pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: To identify/correct deranged coagulation (warfarin, haemophilia, liver impairment).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the difference between a group & save (G&S) and a cross-match?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: G&S: ABO/RhD + atypical antibody screen — if blood might be needed. Cross-match: mix patient + donor blood for compatibility — if blood will be needed; each takes ~40 min; cross-match is done after G&S.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What cardiac investigations are used pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: ECG — CVD history or major surgery; ECHO — murmur, ECG changes, heart failure signs; myocardial perfusion scan — untreated/symptomatic ischaemic heart disease.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What respiratory/functional capacity investigations are used pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Spirometry — pulmonary symptoms or chronic lung disease. CPET (cardiopulmonary exercise test) — high-risk patients undergoing major surgery; a graded cycle test → VO2 max + anaerobic threshold; the best objective measure of functional capacity.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is CPET, and what does it measure?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Cardiopulmonary exercise test — for high-risk patients undergoing major surgery; a graded cycle test giving VO2 max + anaerobic threshold; the best objective measure of functional capacity.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are ASA grades I and II and their mortality?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: I: normal healthy patient (0.1%). II: mild systemic disease (0.2%).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are ASA grades III and IV and their mortality?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: III: severe systemic disease (1.8%). IV: severe systemic disease, a constant threat to life (7.8%).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is ASA grade V and the meaning of the E suffix?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: V: moribund — not expected to survive without surgery (9.4%). E: a suffix added to any grade for an emergency operation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does the ASA grade correlate with?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: It correlates directly with operative mortality (I healthy → V moribund; E suffix = emergency).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is exercise tolerance emphasised pre-operatively, and how is it quantified objectively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: It is the best functional predictor of post-op risk. CPET quantifies it (VO2 max, anaerobic threshold) in high-risk major surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why must morphine be avoided in CKD, and what is the mandatory baseline test?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Avoid morphine in CKD; a U&Es baseline is mandatory to assess renal function.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Mallampati score, and what does it predict?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A pre-operative airway assessment graded I–IV by how much of the soft palate/uvula is visible on mouth opening (I = soft palate, uvula and pillars visible; IV = only the hard palate visible). A higher class predicts a more difficult laryngoscopy/intubation. Assessed alongside thyromental distance, mouth opening, neck mobility and dentition.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does NICE NG45 guide routine pre-operative testing for elective surgery?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Tests are not ordered blanket-fashion but are guided by the patient's ASA grade and the severity of surgery (minor / intermediate / major) — e.g. a healthy ASA 1 patient for minor surgery needs few or no routine tests.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the Three R's of fluid prescribing?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Resuscitation, Replacement, and Maintenance — every fluid prescription begins by identifying which applies.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is resuscitation fluid indicated, and what is given?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: When the patient is in shock/hypovolaemia. A rapid isotonic bolus to restore perfusion.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is replacement fluid indicated?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: When the patient has ongoing abnormal losses (vomiting, NG, stoma, diarrhoea) — maintenance ± adjustments for deficits and losses.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is maintenance fluid indicated, and what are the daily requirements?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: When the patient is NBM but euvolaemic — just covering daily requirements: 25–30 mL/kg water + 1 mmol/kg Na/K/Cl + 50–100 g glucose.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is total body water distributed between intracellular and extracellular compartments?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Intracellular = ⅔ of total body water. Extracellular = ⅓ — split into intravascular (20%) and interstitial (80%).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the third space, and what is third-spacing?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Third space = peritoneal, pleural, pericardial cavities (don't normally hold fluid). Third-spacing = fluid shifts out of vessels into these spaces → hypovolaemia + oedema simultaneously.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the normal serum osmolality?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: 275–295 mOsmol/kg.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is an isotonic fluid, where does it stay, and what is it best for?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Isotonic (saline, Hartmann's) → stays extracellular → best for resuscitation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a hypotonic fluid, where does the water go, and what is it used for?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Hypotonic (5% dextrose, 0.18% saline) → water moves into cells → maintenance only; hyponatraemia risk if overused.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a hypertonic fluid and what does it do?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Hypertonic (3% saline) → pulls water out of cells.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the electrolyte composition of 0.9% saline, and what is its use?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Na+ 154, Cl- 154 mmol/L. Use: resuscitation / maintenance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the electrolyte composition of Hartmann's, and its use?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Na+ 131, K+ 5, Cl- 111 mmol/L. Use: resuscitation / maintenance (balanced).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the composition and use of 0.18% NaCl / 4% glucose?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Na+ 30, Cl- 30 mmol/L, glucose 40 g/L. Use: maintenance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the composition and use of 5% dextrose?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Glucose 50 g/L (no electrolytes). Use: maintenance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 0.9% saline trap, and what is the preferred balanced default?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: 0.9% saline has Na+ 154 (far above plasma 135–145) + Cl- 154 → hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with excess use. Hartmann's is the balanced default — less acidosis risk, surgeons' preferred maintenance fluid.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are colloids, when are they used, and what is albumin's niche?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Colloids (albumin, Gelofusine) — large molecules, stay intravascular longer. Rarely used (anaphylaxis risk; crystalloids equally effective). Albumin has a niche in decompensated liver disease (↑ oncotic pressure).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the signs of hypovolaemia (↓ECF)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Hypotension (SBP <100), tachycardia (>90); CRT >2 s, cold peripheries; ↑RR, dry mucous membranes, ↓skin turgor; ↓urine output, sunken eyes, thirst, ↓weight.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the signs of fluid overload (↑ECF)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Peripheral oedema (ankles/sacrum); pulmonary oedema (SOB, ↓sats, ↑RR, bibasal crackles); raised JVP; ↑weight from baseline (regular weights = key monitoring tool).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What signs does third-spacing produce, and where is it common?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Signs of BOTH simultaneously: empty intravascular compartment (hypovolaemia signs) + oedematous tissues (overload signs). Common in bowel obstruction, peritonitis, burns.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the NICE resuscitation protocol for fluids?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Fluid: 0.9% saline, Hartmann's, or Plasma-Lyte 148 (isotonic). 500 mL bolus over 15 min ("stat"); 250 mL if overload risk (e.g. heart failure). Reassess ABCDE after each bolus. Repeat 250–500 mL boluses as needed. Seek expert help after ~2000 mL if not responding.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does the resuscitation bolus change if there is overload risk?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Give 250 mL (instead of 500 mL) if overload risk (e.g. heart failure).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the potassium safety rule for IV infusion?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: K+ infusion rate must never exceed 10 mmol/hr. Rapid potassium → arrhythmia / cardiac arrest. Never give a rapid bolus with high-potassium bags.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When should you seek senior help during fluid resuscitation?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Get senior help if the patient is shocked or not responding (and after ~2000 mL if not responding). Establish the cause (sepsis, haemorrhage, etc.) alongside resuscitation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the general principles for prescribing maintenance fluids?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Use for the shortest time possible. Stop as soon as oral intake resumes. Calculate on ideal body weight (prevents over-dosing in obese patients).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the daily maintenance requirements (water, electrolytes, glucose)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Water: 25–30 mL/kg. Na+/K+/Cl-: 1 mmol/kg each. Glucose: 50–100 g (anti-ketotic, not nutritional).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the role of glucose in maintenance fluids?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Anti-ketotic, not nutritional (50–100 g/day).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the worked maintenance regimen for a 70 kg patient (target ~2 L / 70 mmol Na+K / 50–100 g glucose)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Bag 1: 500 mL 0.9% saline + 20 mmol K+ over 8 h (all Na, ⅓ K, ¼ water). Bag 2: 1 L 5% dextrose + 20 mmol K+ over 8 h (⅓ K, ½ water, glucose). Bag 3: 500 mL 5% dextrose + 20 mmol K+ over 8 h (⅓ K, ¼ water).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the hyponatraemia risk from hypotonic maintenance fluids, and which fluid reduces it?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: >2.5 L/day of hypotonic fluids (0.18% saline + 4% glucose) → hyponatraemia. Hartmann's is preferred — less hyponatraemia than hypotonic fluids, less hypernatraemia/acidosis than 0.9% saline.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the principle of replacement fluid prescribing?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Replacement = routine maintenance, then add or subtract for existing deficits/excess and ongoing abnormal losses.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is vomiting/NG aspirate high in, and what acid-base consequence results?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: High in H+, Cl-, K+. Causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis → replace K+ + Cl-.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is biliary fluid high in, and what is its acid-base consequence?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: High in Na+, HCO3-. No specific acid-base consequence listed (—).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are pancreatic/jejunal losses high in, and what acid-base consequence results?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: High in Na+, HCO3-. HCO3- loss → metabolic acidosis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are diarrhoea / new stoma losses high in, and what acid-base consequence results?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: High in Na+, K+, HCO3-. Causes metabolic acidosis + hypokalaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Which IV fluid is preferred in a vomiting patient, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: 0.9% saline with added KCl is preferred. Prolonged vomiting/NG loss causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; saline replaces the lost chloride and added potassium corrects the hypokalaemia. Hartmann's is avoided here — its lactate is converted to bicarbonate and would worsen the alkalosis, and its 5 mmol/L K+ is negligible for replacement.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the definition of shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Acute circulatory failure → inadequate tissue oxygen delivery → cellular hypoxia → organ dysfunction. Not simply hypotension.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the DOCH mnemonic for the four types of shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Distributive, Obstructive, Cardiogenic, Hypovolaemic.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and types of distributive shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Mechanism: ↓SVR → maldistributed blood flow. Types: septic (most common), anaphylactic, neurogenic, adrenal.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the haemodynamics, peripheries, and JVP in distributive shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Haemodynamics: ↑CO, ↓SVR, ↓BP. Peripheries: warm, flushed (early sepsis/anaphylaxis); cold (late). JVP: ↓ (low filling pressure).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and types of obstructive shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Mechanism: mechanical obstruction to flow → ↓CO. Types: PE, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, aortic dissection.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the haemodynamics, peripheries, and JVP in obstructive shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Haemodynamics: ↓CO, ↑SVR, ↓BP. Peripheries: cold, clammy. JVP: ↑↑ (obstructed venous return).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and types of cardiogenic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Mechanism: pump failure → ↓CO. Types: MI (especially anterior STEMI), arrhythmia, severe valve disease, myocarditis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the haemodynamics, peripheries, and JVP in cardiogenic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Haemodynamics: ↓CO, ↑SVR, ↓BP. Peripheries: cold, clammy. JVP: ↑ + pulmonary oedema (wet).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and types of hypovolaemic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Mechanism: ↓preload → ↓CO. Types: haemorrhage (see classes), burns, dehydration, 3rd spacing.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the haemodynamics, peripheries, and JVP in hypovolaemic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Haemodynamics: ↓CO, ↑SVR, ↓BP. Peripheries: cold, clammy. JVP: ↓ (reduced filling).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How do the four shock types compare on CO, SVR, JVP, and peripheries?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Distributive: CO ↑, SVR ↓↓, JVP ↓, warm (early). Obstructive: CO ↓, SVR ↑, JVP ↑↑, cold. Cardiogenic: CO ↓↓, SVR ↑, JVP ↑, cold + pulmonary oedema. Hypovolaemic: CO ↓, SVR ↑, JVP ↓↓, cold.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Which shock type has warm peripheries, and what is the key haemodynamic signature?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Only distributive shock has warm peripheries (early); all others are cold and clammy. Distributive = high CO, low SVR.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the approximate blood volume in adults, and what underlies the ATLS haemorrhage classes?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Blood volume ≈ 70 mL/kg (≈5 L for a 70 kg person). Classes are based on blood loss volume and clinical features.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines ATLS Class I haemorrhage?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Blood loss <750 mL (<15%); HR <100; BP normal; RR 14–20; urine output normal (>30 mL/hr); conscious level normal.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines ATLS Class II haemorrhage?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Blood loss 750–1500 mL (15–30%); HR 100–120; BP normal (↑diastolic); RR 20–30; urine output 20–30 mL/hr; anxious.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines ATLS Class III haemorrhage?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Blood loss 1500–2000 mL (30–40%); HR 120–140; BP ↓systolic; RR 30–40; urine output 5–15 mL/hr; confused.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines ATLS Class IV haemorrhage?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Blood loss >2000 mL (>40%); HR >140; BP ↓↓systolic; RR >40; urine output <5 mL/hr; lethargic/unconscious.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is hypotension a late sign in haemorrhage?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: In Class I–II, BP is maintained by compensatory tachycardia + vasoconstriction. BP drops in Class III — by this point ~1.5 L is already lost. Hypotension is a late sign.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is haemorrhagic shock managed (bleeding control, access, fluids)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Stop the bleeding: direct pressure, tourniquet, surgery. 2 large-bore IV cannulae (14–16G), bloods including cross-match. Crystalloid (Hartmann's): 250–500 mL boluses; reassess after each.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is the Major Haemorrhage Protocol activated, and what is the blood product ratio?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Class III–IV: activate Major Haemorrhage Protocol → packed RBCs + FFP + platelets (1:1:1).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the BP targets in haemorrhage (permissive hypotension vs normotension)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Target: SBP 80–90 mmHg in penetrating trauma (permissive hypotension until haemostasis); normotension in TBI/spinal injury.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the role and timing of tranexamic acid in trauma?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Tranexamic acid (TXA) 1 g IV within 3 h of injury (reduces mortality).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the lethal triad of trauma, and how is the cycle broken?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Hypothermia (impairs clotting enzymes; warm ALL fluids, warm patient), acidosis (from tissue hypoxia + lactate; worsens coagulopathy), coagulopathy (dilution from crystalloid, DIC, hypothermia). Each worsens the others → vicious cycle. Damage control surgery + early blood products break the cycle.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Sepsis-3 definition (2016) of sepsis and septic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock: sepsis + vasopressors needed to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the three qSOFA criteria, and what does a score ≥2 mean?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: RR ≥22 breaths/min; altered mentation (GCS <15); SBP ≤100 mmHg. Score ≥2 → suspect sepsis, investigate further. Does NOT replace SOFA but useful outside ICU.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the SOFA organ dysfunction markers across systems?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Respiratory: PaO2/FiO2 <400. Renal: creatinine rising, UO <0.5 mL/kg/hr. Liver: bilirubin rising. Coagulation: platelets falling. CNS: GCS falling. Cardiovascular: MAP <70 or vasopressors needed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Sepsis Six (all within 1 hour)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Give 3: O2 (15 L via NRM, target SpO2 94–98%), IV antibiotics (broad-spectrum within 1 h), IV fluids (500 mL–1 L crystalloid bolus if hypotensive/lactate ↑). Take 3: blood cultures (before antibiotics, 2 sets), lactate + bloods (FBC, CRP, U&E, LFTs, glucose, clotting, VBG lactate), urine output (catheterise, target >0.5 mL/kg/hr).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why must antibiotics be given quickly in sepsis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 h — every hour of delay doubles mortality.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is done if a septic patient is not responding to initial management?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line, via central line; target MAP ≥65 mmHg) → ICU. Consider hydrocortisone 200 mg/day in refractory septic shock.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and common triggers of anaphylactic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: IgE-mediated (Type I hypersensitivity) → massive mast cell degranulation → histamine, tryptase → ↓SVR + bronchospasm + ↑vascular permeability. Triggers: drugs (penicillin, NSAIDs), foods (nuts), latex, stings.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the clinical features of anaphylaxis (skin, airway, breathing, circulation)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Skin: urticaria, erythema, angioedema (lips, tongue, throat). Airway: stridor, hoarseness (laryngeal oedema). Breathing: bronchospasm, wheeze, ↑RR. Circulation: tachycardia, ↓BP, warm flushed skin. ± nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the FIRST drug and dose in anaphylaxis management (Resus Council 2021)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Remove trigger; IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh — FIRST. Repeat at 5 min if no improvement.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the adjunctive treatments in anaphylaxis after adrenaline?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: High-flow O2 via non-rebreathe mask; call for help; IV fluid bolus (500 mL–1 L crystalloid, titrated to response). Per Resuscitation Council UK 2021, corticosteroids and antihistamines are NO LONGER part of routine emergency management — an antihistamine may be considered after stabilisation for persistent skin symptoms only. Observe for a biphasic reaction and discharge with a self-injectable adrenaline device + allergy/immunology referral.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is serum tryptase used in anaphylaxis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Take at 1–2 h and 24 h after the reaction. Elevated tryptase confirms mast cell activation. Send to immunology.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the commonest cause and mortality of cardiogenic shock, and the fluid paradox?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Most commonly from acute anterior STEMI (LV pump failure). Mortality 40–50%. Paradox: giving fluids may worsen pulmonary oedema.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is cardiogenic shock diagnosed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: SBP <90 mmHg AND CO/CI reduced AND adequate filling pressure; cold, clammy, ↑JVP, S3 gallop, pulmonary crackles; ECG: STEMI, new LBBB; Echo: confirms low EF, wall motion abnormality; troponin ↑, BNP ↑.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is cardiogenic shock managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Revascularisation ASAP — primary PCI if MI; this is the definitive treatment. Vasopressors: noradrenaline (MAP ≥65) ± dobutamine (inotrope). Avoid fluids if pulmonary oedema present. Furosemide if fluid overloaded. IABP/Impella (mechanical circulatory support) in refractory cases. ICU admission.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does tension pneumothorax present and how is it treated immediately?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Distinguishing features: tracheal deviation (away), absent breath sounds, ↑JVP, hyper-resonance, hypoxia. Immediate Rx: immediate needle decompression (2nd ICS, MCL) → chest drain.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does cardiac tamponade present (Beck's triad) and how is it treated immediately?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Beck's triad: ↓BP + ↑JVP + muffled heart sounds. Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg. Echocardiography confirms. Immediate Rx: pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid, ultrasound-guided).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does massive PE present and how is it treated immediately?
