Femoral hernias have a cough impulse and inguinal do not
Inguinal hernias only occur in women
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Inguinal is superomedial and femoral is inferolateral to the pubic tubercle
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: The single highest-yield discriminator is location relative to the pubic tubercle: inguinal = superomedial, femoral = inferolateral.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Why does a narrow neck make a hernia high-risk?
options: It widens the defect over time
It improves blood supply to the sac
The bowel gets trapped and cannot decompress
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: The bowel gets trapped and cannot decompress
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Neck width drives risk: a wide neck reduces easily (lower risk), while a narrow neck is high risk because the bowel gets trapped and cannot decompress.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A hernia is now a firm, tender lump that will not reduce, but there is no vomiting or systemic upset. Which stage is this?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Incarceration
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Incarceration is an irreducible hernia — bowel trapped in the sac that cannot be reduced, presenting as a firm, tender lump that won't reduce; it is a precursor to obstruction.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient with a hernia develops vomiting, generalised pain and absolute constipation. Which stage is this?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Obstruction
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Obstruction occurs when trapped bowel blocks faecal flow, presenting with vomiting, generalised pain and absolute constipation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A hernia becomes acutely severely painful and tender at the site. What is happening, and how quickly can it progress?
options: Strangulation — the neck cuts off blood supply, causing infarction within hours
Incarceration — bowel is simply trapped with no ischaemia
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Strangulation — the neck cuts off blood supply, causing infarction within hours
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Strangulation occurs when the neck cuts off the blood supply → ischaemia → infarction, presenting with severe pain and tenderness at the site; it is a surgical emergency that infarcts within hours.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the preferred elective repair for a hernia?
options: Tension repair pulling the defect edges together
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Tension-free repair with mesh
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Tension-free repair (mesh over the defect, reinforced by tissue ingrowth) is preferred. Tension repair pulls the defect edges together but is painful with high recurrence and rarely used.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which hernia is always repaired surgically regardless of symptoms, and why?
options: Umbilical in neonates — they rarely resolve
Femoral — a narrow rigid ring gives a high strangulation risk
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Femoral — a narrow rigid ring gives a high strangulation risk
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: All femoral hernias are repaired surgically regardless, because the narrow, rigid femoral ring gives a high strangulation risk.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What proportion of inguinal hernias are indirect, and what is the sex predominance overall?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: 80% indirect; ~95% male
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Inguinal hernias are ~95% male; indirect account for 80% and direct 20%.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How does an indirect inguinal hernia relate to the inferior epigastric vessels, and what is its origin?
options: Medial to the vessels; acquired wall weakness
Lateral to the vessels; acquired wall weakness
Lateral to the vessels; congenital (patent processus vaginalis)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Lateral to the vessels; congenital (patent processus vaginalis)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: An indirect inguinal hernia passes through the inguinal canal lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and is congenital (failure of the processus vaginalis to obliterate).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: On the deep-ring (occlusion) test, which finding indicates a direct inguinal hernia?
options: It re-bulges despite pressure held over the deep ring
It stays reduced when pressure is held over the deep ring
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: It re-bulges despite pressure held over the deep ring
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: A direct hernia re-bulges despite deep-ring pressure (it arises medially at Hesselbach's triangle), whereas an indirect hernia stays reduced when pressure is held over the deep ring.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Through which mechanism does a direct inguinal hernia occur?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Weakness at Hesselbach's triangle
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: A direct inguinal hernia occurs through a weakness at Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What are the borders of Hesselbach's triangle (R-I-P)?
options: Femoral vein, lacunar ligament, pectineal ligament
Linea alba, semilunar line, arcuate line
Obturator foramen, lacunar ligament, femoral vein
Rectus abdominis, inferior epigastric vessels, Poupart's (inguinal) ligament
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Rectus abdominis, inferior epigastric vessels, Poupart's (inguinal) ligament
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle (R-I-P) is bordered by rectus abdominis (medial), inferior epigastric vessels (lateral) and Poupart's/inguinal ligament (inferior).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What are the borders of the femoral canal (F-L-I-P)?
options: Femoral artery (lateral), inguinal ligament (medial), lacunar ligament (anterior), rectus (posterior)
Femoral vein (lateral), lacunar ligament (medial), inguinal ligament (anterior), pectineal ligament (posterior)
Rectus abdominis, inferior epigastric vessels, Poupart's ligament
Femoral nerve (lateral), pectineal ligament (medial), lacunar ligament (anterior)
Lacunar ligament (lateral), femoral vein (medial), pectineal ligament (anterior)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Femoral vein (lateral), lacunar ligament (medial), inguinal ligament (anterior), pectineal ligament (posterior)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: The femoral canal borders (F-L-I-P) are the femoral vein (lateral), lacunar ligament (medial), inguinal ligament (anterior) and pectineal ligament (posterior).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which is part of the differential for a groin lump?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Saphena varix
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: The groin-lump differential includes femoral hernia, lymph node, saphena varix, femoral aneurysm and undescended testis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A femoral hernia is commoner in which group?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Women, especially multiparous
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Femoral hernias pass through the femoral canal inferolateral to the pubic tubercle and are commoner in women, especially multiparous women.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which hernia occurs at a previous surgical scar and has a high recurrence rate?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Incisional
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: An incisional hernia occurs at a previous surgical scar; it has a high recurrence rate and is often managed conservatively.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How does an umbilical hernia differ from a paraumbilical hernia?
options: Umbilical is asymmetrical below the umbilicus; paraumbilical is through it
Both pass through the linea alba only
Umbilical occurs only at surgical scars
Umbilical is a symmetrical bulge through the umbilicus; paraumbilical is asymmetrical just above/below it (not through)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Umbilical is a symmetrical bulge through the umbilicus; paraumbilical is asymmetrical just above/below it (not through)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: An umbilical hernia is a symmetrical bulge through the umbilicus (neonates often self-resolve, also older adults), whereas a paraumbilical hernia is an asymmetrical bulge just above/below the umbilicus, not through it.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: An epigastric hernia must be distinguished from which condition that is not a true hernia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Divarication of recti
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: An epigastric hernia passes through linea alba fibres; its differential is divarication of recti, which is not a true hernia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which hernia is rare, sits at the semilunar line, and has a high strangulation risk (often missed clinically)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Spigelian
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: A Spigelian hernia is rare, at the semilunar line (lateral rectus border, ~arcuate line), presenting as a small tender mass with a high strangulation risk; it is often missed clinically.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: An elderly multiparous woman with recent rapid weight loss has medial thigh/knee pain on internal rotation of the hip. Which hernia and sign does this represent?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Obturator hernia — Howship–Romberg sign
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: An obturator hernia passes through the obturator foramen (elderly multiparous women + rapid weight loss); the Howship–Romberg sign is medial thigh/knee pain on internal rotation of the hip from obturator nerve compression — a classic SBA clue.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How does a hiatus hernia disrupt normal physiology?
options: It blocks the pylorus, causing vomiting
Widening of the hiatus disrupts the LOS, causing reflux
It cuts off the spermatic cord blood supply
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Widening of the hiatus disrupts the LOS, causing reflux
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: In a hiatus hernia the stomach herniates through the diaphragm into the thorax; widening of the normally narrow, fixed hiatus disrupts the LOS, causing reflux.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which is the commonest type of hiatus hernia, and what does it cause?
options: Type 2 (rolling) — the GOJ stays put, causing GORD
Type 4 — large defect, causing reflux only
Type 2 (rolling) — the commonest, low strangulation risk
Type 1 (sliding) — the GOJ slides up, causing GORD
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Type 1 (sliding) — the GOJ slides up, causing GORD
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Type 1 (sliding) is the commonest hiatus hernia; the GOJ slides up into the thorax with the fundus, causing GORD.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which hiatus hernia type carries a higher strangulation risk because the fundus rolls up while the GOJ stays put?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Type 2 (rolling / paraoesophageal)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Type 2 (rolling/paraoesophageal) has the fundus rolling up alongside the oesophagus with the GOJ staying put, carrying a higher strangulation risk.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the surgical management for a high-risk or refractory hiatus hernia?
options: Laparoscopic fundoplication — wrap the fundus to tighten the LOS
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Laparoscopic fundoplication — wrap the fundus to tighten the LOS
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: A hiatus hernia is managed conservatively (treat GORD with PPI and lifestyle); if high-risk or refractory, laparoscopic fundoplication wraps the fundus around the lower oesophagus to tighten the LOS.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A man has a reducible groin lump that lies superomedial to the pubic tubercle. When pressure is held over the deep ring, the lump stays reduced. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Indirect inguinal hernia
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: A superomedial groin lump is inguinal; staying reduced under deep-ring pressure indicates an indirect hernia (passing through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A woman presents with a tender, irreducible lump inferolateral to the pubic tubercle and signs of bowel obstruction. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Conservative management, as femoral hernias rarely complicate
Elective tension repair in a few weeks
Emergency surgery — femoral hernias have a high strangulation risk and are always repaired
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Emergency surgery — femoral hernias have a high strangulation risk and are always repaired
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: An inferolateral, irreducible, tender groin lump with obstruction is a complicated femoral hernia. Femoral hernias have a high strangulation risk from the narrow rigid ring and are always repaired surgically; with obstruction/strangulation this is an emergency.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the principle behind the post-operative pyrexia 5 Ws?
options: All post-op fevers are caused by wound infection
The site of surgery is irrelevant to fever
Timing of fever narrows the differential before examining the patient
Fever should be ignored in the first week
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Timing of fever narrows the differential before examining the patient
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: The 5 Ws principle is that the timing of fever narrows the differential before examination: early fever = respiratory; later fever = wound/VTE/collection.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient develops a fever on day 1 post-op. Which 'W' and cause is most likely?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Wind — atelectasis/pneumonia
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Day 0–2 fever is 'Wind' — atelectasis or pneumonia; the key action is analgesia, chest physio, mobilisation and deep breathing.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A fever on day 4 with unilateral leg swelling corresponds to which 'W'?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Walking — DVT/PE
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Day 4–6 fever is 'Walking' — DVT/PE; the key action is Doppler USS leg, CTPA, LMWH and TEDs.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which 'W' covers fever from a drug reaction, transfusion reaction or line/cannula sepsis at any time?
options: Wonder drugs / What's in the line
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Wonder drugs / What's in the line
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: The 'Wonder drugs / What's in the line' W can occur at any time and covers drug reaction, transfusion reaction and line/cannula sepsis; the action is to review the drug chart, change/remove lines and take blood cultures.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Why must post-operative haemorrhage be recognised early despite a normal blood pressure?
options: BP is maintained until Class III shock (>1.5 L lost)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: BP is maintained until Class III shock (>1.5 L lost)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Haemorrhage must be recognised fast because BP is maintained until Class III shock (>1.5 L lost); untreated it leads to hypovolaemic shock with tachycardia, falling BP and pale/clammy skin.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient bleeds within 24 hours of surgery as their blood pressure normalises. Which type of haemorrhage is this?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Reactive
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Reactive haemorrhage occurs within 24 h from a slipped ligature or missed vessel as BP normalises post-op. Primary is intra-operative; secondary occurs at 7–10 days when infection erodes a vessel.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient develops sudden haemorrhage into a previously healing wound at day 8. What type is this, and what is the underlying mechanism?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Secondary — infection erodes a vessel
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Secondary haemorrhage occurs at 7–10 days when infection erodes a vessel, often presenting as sudden haemorrhage into a previously healing wound; management is infection control plus surgical re-exploration.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the commonest cause of early post-operative fever (day 0–2)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Atelectasis
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Atelectasis is the commonest early fever (day 0–2): collapse of lung segments from under-ventilation, with fever, raised RR, low SpO2 and reduced basal air entry.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How does the analgesia link reduce respiratory complications?
options: Adequate pain relief allows deep breathing and mobilisation, reducing atelectasis and pneumonia
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Adequate pain relief allows deep breathing and mobilisation, reducing atelectasis and pneumonia
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Adequate pain relief allows deep breathing and mobilisation, reducing atelectasis and pneumonia; under-treated pain causes shallow breathing, retained secretions and infection.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which investigation confirms a suspected post-operative pulmonary embolism?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: CTPA
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: CTPA confirms PE; Doppler USS confirms DVT, and D-dimer is part of the work-up. Prevention is LMWH + TED stockings + early mobilisation, and treatment is therapeutic LMWH → DOAC.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which arrhythmia is especially associated with the post-operative period?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: New atrial fibrillation
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: New AF is especially common post-op, triggered by sympathetic activation, hypoxia and electrolyte disturbance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: When does a post-operative myocardial infarction typically peak?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: 2–3 days post-op
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: ACS/MI from surgical stress unmasking coronary disease peaks 2–3 days post-op; assess with troponin and ECG.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How does post-operative ileus differ fundamentally from mechanical obstruction?
options: Ileus is always caused by adhesions
Ileus shows decompressed distal bowel on AXR
Ileus is functional bowel dysmotility, not mechanical obstruction
Ileus causes high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Ileus is functional bowel dysmotility, not mechanical obstruction
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Ileus is functional bowel dysmotility, not mechanical obstruction; it is common after abdominal/pelvic surgery, long anaesthetics, opioids and electrolyte disturbance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How does the AXR appearance of ileus differ from mechanical obstruction?
options: Ileus shows dilated proximal, decompressed distal; obstruction shows dilated loops throughout
Ileus shows no bowel gas at all
Ileus shows dilated loops throughout; obstruction shows dilated proximal, decompressed distal
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Ileus shows dilated loops throughout; obstruction shows dilated proximal, decompressed distal
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: On AXR, ileus shows dilated loops throughout, whereas obstruction shows dilated proximal and decompressed distal bowel.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How is post-operative ileus managed?
options: Drip & suck (IV fluids + NGT), correct electrolytes especially K+, mobilise, avoid opioids
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Drip & suck (IV fluids + NGT), correct electrolytes especially K+, mobilise, avoid opioids
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Ileus is managed conservatively with drip & suck (IV fluids + NGT), correcting electrolytes (especially K+), mobilisation and avoiding opioids if possible; no surgery is needed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient on day 6 after bowel surgery has increasing pain, fever, peritonism and a sharply rising CRP, with faeculent drain output. What is the most likely complication and confirmatory test?
options: Anastomotic leak; CT abdomen with contrast
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Anastomotic leak; CT abdomen with contrast
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: An anastomotic leak (day 5–7) presents with increasing pain, fever, peritonism, sepsis and faeculent/turbid drain output with a sharply rising CRP; CT abdomen with contrast confirms the leak plus free gas/fluid, and management is resuscitation, IV antibiotics and urgent re-operation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults, as a late post-operative complication?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Adhesions
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Adhesions lead to small bowel obstruction and are the most common cause of SBO in adults; incisional hernia and constipation are other late GI complications.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How is a surgical site infection classified by depth?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Superficial (skin/subcutaneous), deep (fascia/muscle), organ/space
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: SSI is classified as superficial (skin/subcutaneous), deep (fascia/muscle) or organ/space (e.g. intra-abdominal abscess).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What distinguishes a burst abdomen from simple wound dehiscence?
options: Burst abdomen is only partial separation of skin edges
Dehiscence involves bowel protruding through the skin
Burst abdomen is full-thickness separation with bowel/omentum protruding — a surgical emergency
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Burst abdomen is full-thickness separation with bowel/omentum protruding — a surgical emergency
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Dehiscence is partial separation of wound edges, whereas burst abdomen (evisceration) is full-thickness separation with bowel/omentum protruding through skin — a surgical emergency.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient's wound drains serosanguineous 'pink fluid' on day 7. What does this warn of, and how is it managed?
options: Impending burst abdomen; cover bowel with moist sterile dressings and return to theatre urgently
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Impending burst abdomen; cover bowel with moist sterile dressings and return to theatre urgently
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Serosanguineous 'pink fluid' draining from the wound (day 5–10) is the warning sign of burst abdomen; management is to cover the bowel with moist sterile dressings, return urgently to theatre, and perform mass closure with non-absorbable sutures.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the most common nosocomial infection post-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Catheter-associated UTI
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Catheter-associated UTI is the most common nosocomial infection post-op, presenting with dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain and cloudy urine ± systemic sepsis; the catheter should be removed as soon as possible.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A man cannot pass urine after pelvic surgery and opioid analgesia. What is the appropriate next step?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Trial without catheter (TWOC) after catheterisation
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Post-op urinary retention is common (opioids, spinal anaesthesia, pelvic surgery) and commoner in men (BPH risk); a trial without catheter (TWOC) is needed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which drugs are recognised nephrotoxic contributors to post-operative AKI?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: NSAIDs, gentamicin and contrast
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Post-op AKI is caused by hypovolaemia, sepsis and nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, gentamicin, contrast), leading to oliguria and rising creatinine; monitor UO and U&Es, with a fluid challenge if hypovolaemic.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the general transfusion threshold for post-operative anaemia?
options: Hb <70–80 g/L (higher threshold if symptomatic or cardiac/respiratory disease)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Hb <70–80 g/L (higher threshold if symptomatic or cardiac/respiratory disease)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Hb <100 g/L is managed with oral/IV iron; transfusion is considered at Hb <70–80 g/L, with a higher threshold if symptomatic or there is cardiac/respiratory disease.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A Jehovah's Witness with capacity has a valid advance directive refusing blood. How should this be managed?
options: Transfuse anyway in their best interests
Respect autonomy; optimise pre-op, use cell salvage and minimise intra-op loss
Obtain consent from the next of kin to transfuse
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Respect autonomy; optimise pre-op, use cell salvage and minimise intra-op loss
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: A Jehovah's Witness may refuse transfusion by a valid advance directive; autonomy is respected if capacity is present, and management focuses on optimising pre-op, using cell salvage and minimising intra-op loss.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which factors make up the Apfel score for PONV?
options: Male, smoker, no PONV history, NSAIDs
Female, non-smoker, prior PONV/motion sickness, post-op opioids
Length of surgery, type of incision, blood loss, anaemia
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Female, non-smoker, prior PONV/motion sickness, post-op opioids
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: The Apfel score factors are female sex, non-smoker, prior PONV/motion sickness and post-op opioids (each 1 point; ≥3 = high risk); prophylaxis is ondansetron + dexamethasone at induction, with TIVA instead of volatile agents.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What do the reversible causes of post-operative delirium (PINCH ME) include?
options: Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: PINCH ME = Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment; also exclude hypoxia, sepsis, urinary retention and hypoglycaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which drug class should be avoided in post-operative delirium because it worsens the condition?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Benzodiazepines
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Delirium is managed by treating the cause and reorienting; antipsychotics are avoided unless there is severe agitation, and benzodiazepines are avoided because they worsen delirium.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: When is TPN (total parenteral nutrition) indicated post-operatively?
options: As first-line for all post-op patients
Whenever the patient declines oral food
Instead of early enteral feeding in ERAS
Only when the GI tract is completely unusable; it is given via a central line
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Only when the GI tract is completely unusable; it is given via a central line
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Enteral feeding is preferred; TPN is used via a central line only if the GI tract is completely unusable, because the hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: In which patients should NSAIDs be avoided on the analgesic ladder?
options: Asthma, renal impairment, cardiac disease and peptic ulcer disease
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Asthma, renal impairment, cardiac disease and peptic ulcer disease
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: On the multimodal analgesic ladder, NSAIDs are avoided in asthma, renal impairment, cardiac disease and peptic ulcer disease.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the key safety mechanism of patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)?
options: Only the patient presses the button — staff/family must not press it
The pump delivers continuous opioid regardless of the patient
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Only the patient presses the button — staff/family must not press it
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: PCA delivers IV opioid on-demand with a lockout interval; the key safety mechanism is that only the patient presses the button, and staff/family must not press it. Naloxone, an antiemetic and atropine should be available.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which medication should be available with PCA to reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Naloxone
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: With PCA, naloxone should be available for respiratory depression, an antiemetic for PONV, and atropine for bradycardia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Why should every line, tube and drain be removed as early as appropriate (ERAS principle)?
options: Devices improve outcomes the longer they stay
Removal is purely a cost-saving measure
Every device left in longer than needed increases infection risk and impairs mobilisation
Catheters reduce the risk of retention
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Every device left in longer than needed increases infection risk and impairs mobilisation
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Under the ERAS principle, every device left in longer than needed increases infection risk and impairs mobilisation, so catheters, drains, cannulae and NGTs are removed as early as appropriate.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient on day 2 post-laparotomy has a fever of 38°C, a respiratory rate of 24, oxygen saturations of 92% and reduced air entry at both bases. CXR shows basal shadowing. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?
options: Atelectasis; adequate analgesia, chest physiotherapy, mobilisation and incentive spirometry
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Atelectasis; adequate analgesia, chest physiotherapy, mobilisation and incentive spirometry
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Day 0–2 fever with raised RR, low SpO2, reduced basal air entry and basal shadowing is atelectasis, the commonest early fever; management is adequate analgesia (allowing deep breathing), chest physiotherapy, mobilisation and incentive spirometry.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: An elderly patient becomes acutely confused with fluctuating cognition on day 3 post-op. What is the best initial approach?
options: Identify and treat reversible causes (PINCH ME), reorient, and avoid benzodiazepines
Sedate heavily with antipsychotics regardless of agitation
Ignore it as a normal post-op finding
Discharge the patient to reduce disorientation
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Identify and treat reversible causes (PINCH ME), reorient, and avoid benzodiazepines
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Post-op delirium (acute fluctuating confusion, common in the elderly/frail) is approached by identifying and treating reversible causes (PINCH ME) and excluding hypoxia, sepsis, urinary retention and hypoglycaemia; reorient, avoid antipsychotics unless severe agitation, and avoid benzodiazepines as they worsen delirium.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Add weak opioid (e.g. codeine)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Step 2 = add weak opioid to existing Step 1 non-opioids.
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient in chronic pain is already on regular paracetamol and ibuprofen but remains in pain. What is the next step on the WHO pain ladder?

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Fentanyl
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Fentanyl is preferred in renal failure — morphine-6-glucuronide accumulates in CKD.
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient with CKD (eGFR 18) requires strong opioid analgesia. Which is most appropriate?

options: Perioral tingling → tinnitus → seizures → cardiovascular collapse
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Perioral tingling → tinnitus → seizures → cardiovascular collapse
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Progressive CNS → cardiovascular toxicity from rising plasma LA levels.
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Signs of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity in order are:

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Intralipid 20%
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Lipid emulsion creates 'lipid sink' sequestering LA and preventing cardiac toxicity.
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Antidote for LA toxicity?

A 70-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer has severe pain uncontrolled on regular codeine 60 mg QDS and paracetamol 1 g QDS. He is drowsy and vomiting. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Convert to SC morphine via syringe driver (step 3 opioid, parenteral route due to vomiting)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Convert to SC morphine via syringe driver (step 3 opioid, parenteral route due to vomiting)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: This patient needs step 3 analgesia (strong opioid) and cannot tolerate oral route (vomiting). SC syringe driver with diamorphine (+ antiemetic such as haloperidol, + midazolam if agitated) is appropriate. Calculate 24-hour morphine equivalent first, then convert to SC diamorphine (÷3).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A 28-year-old woman takes ibuprofen regularly for period pain but now presents with haematemesis. Endoscopy shows a duodenal ulcer. Which mechanism explains NSAIDs causing peptic ulcers?
options: COX-1 inhibition reduces prostaglandin E2, reducing gastric mucus and bicarbonate secretion and increasing acid
COX-2 inhibition only causes GI toxicity
Direct corrosive effect on mucosa only
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: COX-1 inhibition reduces prostaglandin E2, reducing gastric mucus and bicarbonate secretion and increasing acid
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: COX-1 is constitutively expressed and produces cytoprotective prostaglandins (PGE₂, PGI₂) in the stomach — maintaining mucus/bicarbonate barrier and regulating gastric blood flow. NSAIDs block COX-1 → reduced mucosal protection → ulceration. Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) have less GI toxicity.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient presents with pinpoint pupils, GCS 8, and respiratory rate of 6/min after taking multiple opioid tablets. What is the immediate treatment?
options: IV naloxone 0.4 mg repeated every 2–3 minutes until responsive
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: IV naloxone 0.4 mg repeated every 2–3 minutes until responsive
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Classic opioid overdose triad: miosis (pinpoint pupils), respiratory depression, reduced consciousness. Naloxone (μ-opioid antagonist) reverses effects — titrate IV 0.4 mg every 2–3 min. Naloxone half-life is 30–90 min (shorter than many opioids) → may need repeated doses or infusion. Airway management first (ABC).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A 55-year-old woman with diabetic neuropathy has burning pain and allodynia in her feet, inadequately controlled with paracetamol. What is the most appropriate first-line analgesic for neuropathic pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Amitriptyline 10 mg nocte (tricyclic antidepressant)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: NICE recommends amitriptyline (or duloxetine) as first-line for neuropathic pain. TCAs modulate pain by inhibiting serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake in descending inhibitory pathways. Started at low dose (10 mg nocte) to minimise anticholinergic side effects. Pregabalin/gabapentin are alternatives if TCAs not tolerated.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which of the following analgesics should be AVOIDED in a patient with eGFR 20 mL/min?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation in the kidney → reduced glomerular filtration → AKI. In CKD (eGFR <30), NSAIDs are contraindicated — risk of further renal impairment and hyperkalaemia. Paracetamol, fentanyl, and buprenorphine are safer in renal failure.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What are the WHO pain ladder principles (the three 'bys')?
options: By the clock (regular dosing), by the mouth (oral preferred), by the ladder (step-wise escalation)
By the pain score, by the patient, by the nurse
By the weight, by the age, by the route
By the diagnosis, by the side effect, by the dose
By the cancer, by the hospital, by the surgeon
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: By the clock (regular dosing), by the mouth (oral preferred), by the ladder (step-wise escalation)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: WHO pain ladder principles: (1) By the clock — analgesics given at regular intervals (not PRN) for chronic pain; (2) By the mouth — oral route preferred when possible; (3) By the ladder — start at appropriate step and escalate if pain not controlled. A fourth principle added later: for the individual.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A 35-year-old man develops agitation, hyperthermia, tremor, clonus, and diaphoresis after starting tramadol alongside his prescribed sertraline. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Serotonin syndrome
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Serotonin syndrome = excess serotonergic activity: confusion/agitation, hyperthermia, clonus (pathognomonic), myoclonus, diaphoresis, tachycardia. Tramadol (SNRI properties) + SSRI (sertraline) = serotonin toxicity. Stop both drugs; manage with benzodiazepines, cooling; cyproheptadine (5HT₂A antagonist) in severe cases.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What dose of paracetamol is safe in adults?
options: Max 4 g/day (1 g QDS) in healthy adults; reduced to 2 g/day in liver disease, alcoholism, low weight (<50 kg), or malnutrition
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Max 4 g/day (1 g QDS) in healthy adults; reduced to 2 g/day in liver disease, alcoholism, low weight (<50 kg), or malnutrition
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Standard adult paracetamol dose: 1 g every 4–6 hours, max 4 g/24h. Dose reduction (to 2 g/day) in hepatic impairment, chronic alcoholism, malnutrition, or weight <50 kg — these patients have reduced glutathione stores, increasing NAPQI toxicity risk.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is multimodal analgesia and why is it preferred post-operatively?
options: Combining analgesics from different classes (paracetamol + NSAID + opioid + regional block) to achieve opioid-sparing effect and better pain control with fewer side effects
Using one drug class at maximum dose
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Combining analgesics from different classes (paracetamol + NSAID + opioid + regional block) to achieve opioid-sparing effect and better pain control with fewer side effects
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Multimodal analgesia combines drugs acting at different pain pathway targets — reducing overall opioid consumption (opioid-sparing), improving pain scores, reducing opioid side effects (nausea, constipation, respiratory depression). It is the foundation of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A palliative patient is on oral morphine 60 mg/day. She can no longer swallow. What dose of subcutaneous diamorphine should be prescribed over 24 hours?
options: 20 mg SC diamorphine over 24 hours (oral morphine ÷ 3)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: 20 mg SC diamorphine over 24 hours (oral morphine ÷ 3)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Conversion: oral morphine to SC diamorphine = divide by 3. Oral morphine 60 mg → SC diamorphine 20 mg/24 hours via syringe driver. Diamorphine is preferred in UK syringe drivers (highly soluble, compatible with other drugs). In countries without diamorphine, use SC morphine (÷2 from oral).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient on the post-operative ward has a pain score of 8/10 after abdominal surgery. They have received oral co-codamol without relief. What is the most appropriate next analgesic step?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: IV/IM morphine (step 3 strong opioid)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Pain score 8/10 = severe pain uncontrolled on step 2 (co-codamol = codeine + paracetamol). Escalate to step 3: IV or IM morphine (immediate-release). In the post-operative setting, titrated IV morphine is most appropriate for rapid, effective pain relief. Add regular paracetamol and NSAID (if no contraindications) as adjuncts.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What mechanism causes codeine to be ineffective in ~10% of Caucasian patients?
options: CYP2D6 poor metabolisers cannot convert codeine to its active form, morphine
Codeine is renally cleared at a faster rate
Codeine binds to different receptors in these patients
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: CYP2D6 poor metabolisers cannot convert codeine to its active form, morphine
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Codeine is a prodrug — converted to morphine by hepatic CYP2D6. Poor metabolisers (~10% Caucasians) have reduced/absent CYP2D6 activity → codeine remains inactive → no analgesia. Ultra-rapid metabolisers (e.g., Ethiopian/Saudi populations ~10–30%) convert codeine rapidly → excessive morphine → toxicity. Codeine is now contraindicated in children <12 (CYP2D6 variability risk).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the mechanism of action of gabapentin?
options: Binds the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels → reduces calcium influx → reduces neurotransmitter release and neuronal excitability
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Binds the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels → reduces calcium influx → reduces neurotransmitter release and neuronal excitability
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Gabapentin/pregabalin bind the α2δ (alpha-2-delta) subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels — reduces presynaptic calcium entry → less glutamate/substance P release → reduced pain transmission. Effective for neuropathic pain, post-herpetic neuralgia, and as perioperative adjuncts. Also anxiolytic.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What are the side effects of opioid analgesia that must be monitored in a post-operative patient?
options: Respiratory depression (most dangerous), sedation, nausea/vomiting, constipation, urinary retention, pruritus
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Respiratory depression (most dangerous), sedation, nausea/vomiting, constipation, urinary retention, pruritus
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Opioid side effects: respiratory depression (most dangerous — monitor RR and O₂ saturation), sedation, nausea/vomiting (prescribe antiemetics), constipation (prescribe laxatives prophylactically — osmotic + stimulant), urinary retention, pruritus (antihistamines). Miosis (pinpoint pupils) is a sign of toxicity.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A 65-year-old woman on ibuprofen for osteoarthritis is found to have eGFR 35 (CKD stage 3). She also takes ramipril. What drug interaction makes her particularly at risk?
options: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + CKD = 'triple whammy' — markedly increased AKI risk (reduced prostaglandin + reduced angiotensin II = loss of renal autoregulation)
NSAID + ACE inhibitor reduces BP beneficially
NSAIDs are safe in stage 3 CKD
ACE inhibitors protect the kidney from NSAIDs
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + CKD = 'triple whammy' — markedly increased AKI risk (reduced prostaglandin + reduced angiotensin II = loss of renal autoregulation)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: The 'triple whammy' = NSAID (blocks afferent arteriolar prostaglandins) + ACE inhibitor/ARB (blocks efferent arteriolar angiotensin II) + CKD (already reduced reserve) → severe loss of renal autoregulation → AKI. Adding a diuretic makes it a 'quadruple whammy'. NSAIDs should be stopped in this patient.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the maximum daily dose of codeine phosphate?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: 240 mg/day (60 mg QDS)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Codeine phosphate maximum dose is 60 mg per dose, up to 4 times daily = 240 mg/day in adults. At higher doses, risks (respiratory depression, constipation, dependence) outweigh benefits due to the ceiling effect. If pain uncontrolled at maximum codeine, escalate to step 3 strong opioids.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient is started on a fentanyl 25 mcg/hour transdermal patch for chronic pain. When does the patch reach steady-state plasma concentration?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: 24–72 hours after application
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Transdermal fentanyl patches reach steady-state plasma concentration after 24–72 hours (typically ~48 hours). They are changed every 72 hours. During initial titration, breakthrough analgesia (short-acting opioid) must be available for the first 24–48 hours. Patches are suitable for stable chronic pain, not acute pain.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which analgesic is contraindicated in patients with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD/Samter's triad)?
options: NSAIDs (including aspirin) — trigger bronchoconstriction via COX inhibition → shunting to leukotriene pathway
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: NSAIDs (including aspirin) — trigger bronchoconstriction via COX inhibition → shunting to leukotriene pathway
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Samter's triad: aspirin/NSAID sensitivity + chronic sinusitis with nasal polyps + asthma. NSAIDs inhibit COX-1 → arachidonic acid shunted to lipoxygenase pathway → excess leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4) → severe bronchoconstriction. Avoid all NSAIDs. Paracetamol at standard doses is safe; selective COX-2 inhibitors generally safe.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the role of TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) in pain management?
options: Non-pharmacological pain management — stimulates large Aβ fibres to inhibit pain transmission via gate control theory (spinal cord level)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Non-pharmacological pain management — stimulates large Apiβ fibres to inhibit pain transmission via gate control theory (spinal cord level)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: TENS activates large-diameter non-nociceptive Aβ fibres at the dorsal horn — these activate inhibitory interneurons that suppress nociceptive C and Aδ fibre transmission (gate control theory, Melzack and Wall). Used for: chronic musculoskeletal pain, neuropathic pain, labour pain. Non-invasive, safe adjunct.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is buprenorphine's mechanism, and why is it used in opioid dependence treatment?
options: Partial μ-opioid agonist + κ-antagonist — high receptor affinity but partial agonism = ceiling effect on respiratory depression; used as sublingual/transdermal analgesic and (with naloxone as Suboxone) for opioid dependence
Codeine derivative with no receptor affinity
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Partial μ-opioid agonist + κ-antagonist — high receptor affinity but partial agonism = ceiling effect on respiratory depression; used as sublingual/transdermal analgesic and (with naloxone as Suboxone) for opioid dependence
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Buprenorphine: partial μ-agonist (ceiling effect on respiratory depression — safer) + κ-antagonist. Very high receptor affinity (can displace full agonists). Sublingual buprenorphine is analgesic; transdermal patches (Butrans) are used for chronic pain; Suboxone (buprenorphine + naloxone sublingual) is used for opioid dependence substitution therapy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A 12-year-old child post-tonsillectomy requires analgesia. Which opioid is now contraindicated in children under 12 years?
options: Codeine — risk of fatal respiratory depression in CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Codeine — risk of fatal respiratory depression in CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Codeine is contraindicated in children <12 years (and in children with obstructive sleep apnoea). CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers convert codeine to morphine at an accelerated rate → fatal respiratory depression. Multiple deaths reported post-tonsillectomy. MHRA banned codeine for children <12 in 2013.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is an intercostal nerve block used for?
options: Post-thoracotomy pain, rib fractures — local anaesthetic injected below the rib at the intercostal groove, blocking the intercostal nerve
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Post-thoracotomy pain, rib fractures — local anaesthetic injected below the rib at the intercostal groove, blocking the intercostal nerve
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Intercostal nerve blocks are used for thoracic pain (post-thoracotomy, rib fractures) — local anaesthetic is injected at the inferior margin of the rib (where the neurovascular bundle runs). Also used for upper abdominal surgery. Complications: pneumothorax, systemic LA toxicity. TAP block is an alternative for abdominal pain.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient is prescribed regular morphine SR 30 mg BD. What PRN breakthrough analgesia should be prescribed?
options: Morphine IR 10 mg oral PRN 4-hourly (1/6 of 24-hour total: 60 mg/6 = 10 mg)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Morphine IR 10 mg oral PRN 4-hourly (1/6 of 24-hour total: 60 mg/6 = 10 mg)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Breakthrough analgesia = 1/6 of the 24-hour total regular opioid dose. Total daily morphine = 30 mg × 2 = 60 mg. 60 mg ÷ 6 = 10 mg IR morphine PRN. This can be given up to 4-hourly. Review total opioid use daily — if multiple breakthrough doses used, increase background dose.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the mechanism of paracetamol overdose hepatotoxicity?
options: NAPQI accumulation → depletes glutathione → hepatocellular necrosis in centrilobular zone 3
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: NAPQI accumulation → depletes glutathione → hepatocellular necrosis in centrilobular zone 3
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Paracetamol is metabolised (>90%) via glucuronidation/sulphation. A toxic metabolite NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) is produced via CYP450 — normally detoxified by glutathione. Overdose overwhelms glutathione → NAPQI accumulates → centrilobular (zone 3) hepatocellular necrosis. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is the antidote.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the TAP (Transversus Abdominis Plane) block?
options: USS-guided local anaesthetic injection into the plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles — blocks anterior abdominal wall sensory nerves (T6–L1)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: USS-guided local anaesthetic injection into the plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles — blocks anterior abdominal wall sensory nerves (T6–L1)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: TAP block: USS-guided injection into the fascial plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis — bathing the T6–L1 somatic nerves. Effective for lower abdominal surgery (caesarean section, laparoscopic surgery, appendicectomy, hernia repair). Opioid-sparing effect. Part of ERAS protocols.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What condition is associated with 'wind-up' pain and central sensitisation?
options: Fibromyalgia, complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), and chronic widespread pain — central sensitisation means peripheral stimulus produces amplified central pain response
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Fibromyalgia, complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), and chronic widespread pain — central sensitisation means peripheral stimulus produces amplified central pain response
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Central sensitisation: repeated nociceptive input → NMDA receptor activation → spinal cord hyperexcitability ('wind-up') → amplified pain perception. Associated with fibromyalgia, CRPS, IBS, and chronic pain states. Ketamine (NMDA antagonist) and gabapentinoids partially address central sensitisation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient with chronic cancer pain is on step 3 of the WHO ladder with oral oxycodone 80 mg/day but still has breakthrough pain despite maximum doses. What is the next step?
options: Specialist palliative care referral — consider interventional techniques (epidural, intrathecal pump, coeliac plexus block) or opioid rotation
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Specialist palliative care referral — consider interventional techniques (epidural, intrathecal pump, coeliac plexus block) or opioid rotation
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: When step 3 opioids are inadequate despite optimisation, the 'fourth step' = interventional pain management. Options: opioid rotation (switching to different opioid — incomplete cross-tolerance), epidural/intrathecal opioids (more potent, lower systemic dose), coeliac plexus neurolysis for pancreatic cancer pain. Specialist palliative care involvement is essential.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: EXAM PEARL: What are the WHO analgesic ladder principles and what defines each step?
options: Step 1=non-opioids; Step 2=weak opioids±non-opioids; Step 3=strong opioids±non-opioids; Adjuvants at all steps; Principles: by mouth, by clock, by ladder
Step 1=mild pain, Step 2=moderate pain, Step 3=severe pain regardless of drug class
No fixed steps — titrate based on pain score alone
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Step 1=non-opioids; Step 2=weak opioids±non-opioids; Step 3=strong opioids±non-opioids; Adjuvants at all steps; Principles: by mouth, by clock, by ladder
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: WHO analgesic ladder (1986): Step 1 = paracetamol/NSAIDs (mild pain); Step 2 = codeine/tramadol ± non-opioids (moderate pain); Step 3 = morphine/oxycodone/fentanyl ± non-opioids (severe pain). Adjuvants (antidepressants, anticonvulsants, steroids) added at any step for specific pain types. Principles: oral route preferred, regular dosing ('by the clock'), step-wise escalation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient on long-term opioids has constipation not responding to lactulose and senna. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Methylnaltrexone (peripheral μ-opioid receptor antagonist) — does not cross BBB, treats opioid-induced constipation without reversing analgesia
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Methylnaltrexone (peripheral μ-opioid receptor antagonist) — does not cross BBB, treats opioid-induced constipation without reversing analgesia
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Methylnaltrexone (Relistor): peripherally acting μ-opioid receptor antagonist — blocks GI opioid receptors causing constipation without crossing the blood-brain barrier, so does not reverse central analgesia. Indicated for opioid-induced constipation (OIC) unresponsive to standard laxatives. Also: naloxegol (oral), alvimopan.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the role of dexamethasone in cancer pain?
options: Reduces peritumoral oedema around nerve/cord compression → reduces neuropathic pain; also antiemetic, appetite stimulant
Causes pain relief through its antihistamine effect
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Reduces peritumoral oedema around nerve/cord compression → reduces neuropathic pain; also antiemetic, appetite stimulant
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) are key adjuvants in cancer pain: reduce oedema around tumour/nerve compression (especially spinal cord compression and cerebral metastases), have antiemetic properties, and improve appetite. Given at the highest effective dose for the shortest period to minimise Cushingoid side effects.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the maximum dose of oral ibuprofen for analgesia in adults?
options: 400 mg TDS–QDS (max 2.4 g/day for analgesia; 3.2 g/day for anti-inflammatory in rheumatology)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: 400 mg TDS–QDS (max 2.4 g/day for analgesia; 3.2 g/day for anti-inflammatory in rheumatology)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Ibuprofen OTC dose: 200–400 mg TDS (max 1.2 g/day OTC). Prescription analgesic dose: up to 400 mg QDS (max 2.4 g/day). Higher doses (max 3.2 g/day) used in rheumatology for anti-inflammatory effect. GI protection (PPI) recommended for doses >1.2 g/day or in at-risk patients.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is phantom limb pain and what is the most effective treatment?
options: Pain perceived in an amputated limb — treated with mirror therapy, gabapentin/pregabalin, amitriptyline, and TENS; mechanism involves cortical reorganisation and central sensitisation
Nociceptive pain from the stump only
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Pain perceived in an amputated limb — treated with mirror therapy, gabapentin/pregabalin, amitriptyline, and TENS; mechanism involves cortical reorganisation and central sensitisation
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Phantom limb pain: perceived pain in the removed limb — affects ~80% of amputees. Mechanism: cortical reorganisation after amputation + central sensitisation. Mirror therapy (visual feedback tricks the brain) is the most evidence-based non-pharmacological approach. Pharmacological: gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline, ketamine. NSAIDs/simple opioids are largely ineffective.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the gate control theory of pain (Melzack and Wall)?
options: Large-diameter Aβ fibres (non-nociceptive) inhibit transmission of small-diameter C and Aδ (nociceptive) fibres at the spinal cord dorsal horn via interneurons — 'closing the gate'
Opioids close the gate via receptor binding
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Large-diameter Aβ fibres (non-nociceptive) inhibit transmission of small-diameter C and Aδ (nociceptive) fibres at the spinal cord dorsal horn via interneurons — 'closing the gate'
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Gate control theory (1965): non-nociceptive sensory input (Aβ fibres) activates inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn → suppresses nociceptive transmission from Aδ (sharp pain) and C (burning pain) fibres → 'gates' close → reduced pain perception. Explains rubbing an injury and the mechanism of TENS, acupuncture, and spinal cord stimulation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the difference between acute and chronic pain in terms of pathophysiology?
options: Acute = protective nociceptive signal from tissue damage (heals with injury); Chronic = persistent pain beyond tissue healing (>3 months) involving central sensitisation, neuroplasticity
Acute = always severe; Chronic = always mild
Acute requires no treatment; Chronic requires opioids
Acute is neuropathic; Chronic is nociceptive
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Acute = protective nociceptive signal from tissue damage (heals with injury); Chronic = persistent pain beyond tissue healing (>3 months) involving central sensitisation, neuroplasticity
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Acute pain: adaptive signal from tissue damage → motivates protective behaviour → resolves with healing. Chronic pain (>3 months): maladaptive — involves central sensitisation (NMDA, wind-up), neuroplasticity, psychosocial factors (catastrophising, depression). Treated differently: chronic pain requires biopsychosocial approach, not just dose escalation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient with sickle cell disease presents in vaso-occlusive crisis with severe pain (10/10). What is the most appropriate immediate analgesic?
options: IV opioid analgesia (morphine) titrated to pain score, given promptly
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: IV opioid analgesia (morphine) titrated to pain score, given promptly
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis causes severe ischaemic bone/organ pain — requires prompt strong opioid analgesia (IV morphine or hydromorphone). NICE and British Society for Haematology guidelines emphasise immediate analgesia within 30 minutes. Also: analgesia within 30 min of presentation, IV fluids, oxygen if hypoxic, anti-inflammatory adjuncts.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the first-line pharmacological treatment for neuropathic pain in a non-cancer patient (NICE guidelines)?
options: Amitriptyline or duloxetine (TCAs/SNRIs) first-line; gabapentin/pregabalin as alternatives
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Amitriptyline or duloxetine (TCAs/SNRIs) first-line; gabapentin/pregabalin as alternatives
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: NICE NG173 (Chronic Pain 2021) and CKS for neuropathic pain: amitriptyline or duloxetine are first-line for non-specialist management. Pregabalin or gabapentin are alternatives (note: gabapentinoids have abuse potential — schedule 3 controlled drugs in UK since 2019). Topical capsaicin for localised neuropathic pain. Opioids are not first-line for neuropathic pain.
